abstract: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) represents a conserved immune strategy enabling plants to mount long-lasting, whole-plant protection following localized pathogen challenge. In Arabidopsis thaliana, SAR is orchestrated by the mobile immune regulator N-hydroxypipecolic acid (NHP); however, the extent to which NHP defines systemic immune states in polyploid crops remains unclear. Here, we establish NHP as an inducer of systemic immunity in hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum) during infection by the obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia triticina. Local NHP application conferred robust disease suppression in distal leaves and elicited a temporally structured oxidative response characterized by a distal, biphasic reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave linking local and systemic tissues. RNA-sequencing analysis revealed that NHP induces coordinated transcriptional reprogramming, characterized by systemic activation of pattern-triggered and effector-triggered immunity pathways, WRKY-centered transcriptional networks, NPR1-associated signaling, and broad-spectrum resistance loci including Lr34. Concomitantly, targeted metabolomic profiling revealed a unique systemic accumulation of salicylic acid, salicylic acid glucoside, pipecolic acid, and NHP, without the conventional jasmonate signaling antagonism observed in eudicots. Despite this conserved immune architecture, functional analyses indicated divergence within the NHP biosynthetic pathway; while a single wheat FMO from sub-clade A2 was systemically up-regulated by NHP, the highly conserved TaSARD4 homeologs were constitutively expressed and functionally dispensable for rust resistance in planta. Notably, heterologous expression of TaSARD4-B successfully restored NHP-glucoside accumulation in an Arabidopsis sard4 mutant, confirming biochemical competence and suggesting alternative metabolic redundancies in wheat. These findings define a systems-level NHP-driven immune state in wheat and provide a conceptual framework for dissecting systemic immunity in cereals, extending SAR paradigms beyond model plant systems.
